background.definition: Acute mosquito-borne disease caused by infection and destruction of red blood cells by 1 of 5 forms of the genus Plasmodium.

list.listitem: About 2000 cases of malaria are diagnosed annually in the United States; the vast majority in travelers and immigrants from endemic areas.
1.5 per 1000 for travelers to Africa
0.11 per 1000 for travelers to Asia.
0.04 per 1000 for travelers to Central/South America.

Authors of a meta-analysis of imported cases of malaria to non-endemic countries found that the west African region accounted for 56% (13,947/24,941) of all imported cases with France and the UK receiving the highest number of cases (>4000 reported cases, on average, annually).

Between May-October 2023, 10 locally-acquired cases of malaria were reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) including seven cases of P. vivax malaria in Sarasota County, FL, one case (P. vivax) in Cameron County, TX, one case (P. vivax) in Saline County, Arkansas, and one case of P. falciparum malaria in a Maryland resident who lives in the National Capital Region. All patients were treated at area hospitals and have recovered.
According to the CDC, an estimated 241 million cases of malaria occurred worldwide in 2020, with 627,000 deaths, most among children in sub-Saharan Africa. This represents an increase from 2018.
Most malaria cases and deaths in 2018 were in Africa (93% and 94%, respectively), with Nigeria accounting for 25% of total cases.
Children 5 years and younger are the most vulnerable group affected by malaria, accounting for 67% (272,000) of all malaria deaths worldwide in 2018.
Approximately $12 billion annually in Africa.

In Nigeria alone, malaria is estimated to affect the gross domestic product by 40% annually and cost approximately US $1.5 billion in out-of-pocket treatments, prevention, costs, and loss of work hours.
Almost no economic impact in the United States.
Malaria is the deadliest parasitic disease.
In less developed nations, malaria is the fourth leading cause of death in children.

Between 2005 to 2015, however, there was a significant decrease in mortality rates due to malaria globally (43.1%; 95% CI, 34.7-51.8). Communicable, maternal, neonatal, and nutritional diseases caused the most years of life lost throughout sub-Saharan Africa, especially for countries in which malaria or HIV/AIDS remained the leading causes of early death.
Among low socioeconomic index countries, 20-30% of total disability is largely attributable to nutritional deficiencies, malaria, neglected tropical diseases, HIV/AIDS, and tuberculosis.
In Ghana, the odds ratio for risk of stillbirth in women with malaria was 1.9 (95% CI, 1.2-9.3).
Plasmodium falciparum.
Plasmodium vivax.
Plasmodium ovale.
Plasmodium malariae.
Of these species, Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax pose the greatest threat.
Plasmodium vivax is the prevailing parasite in the western hemisphere, representing 75% of malaria cases.
Risk factors include travel to endemic areas and length of stay in high-risk areas.

Locally-transmitted mosquito-borne malaria in the US is rare, with only 63 outbreaks occurring between 1957 and 2015, according to the CDC. Transfusion-transmitted malaria is also rare in the US, with only 97 cases reported between 1963 and 2015.

Though malaria is a parasitic mosquito-borne infection most commonly, Plasmodium can also be transmitted to humans by direct inoculation of infected red blood cells via transfusion, needles, and congenitally.
Humans are infected through Anopheles mosquito bites.

After injection of Plasmodium sporozoites (often 10-100) into the host during a blood meal, the sporozoites first infect hepatocytes and replicate to form thousands of merozoites (Primary Liver Stage). Upon rupture of the infected hepatocytes, these merozoites enter the circulation and can infect red blood cells. Once inside red blood cells, merozoites develop into trophozoites, then divide and develop into new merozoites. Eventually the red cell will rupture and further merozoites are released into circulation (Erythrocytic/ Blood Phase). This cycle may take 24-72 hours depending on the species, and can continue to repeat itself. This cycling also corresponds to the cyclic fevers that some, but not all, patients experience.
Disease severity is often proportional to the number of circulating merozoites in the patient, but some P. falciparum infections can become severe in lower ranges.

Time from initial infection to symptom presentation will vary across Plasmodium sps. For instance, P. knowlesi and P. falciparum incubation is often 9-14 days, while P. vivax ranges from 12-17 days, and P. ovale ranges from 16-18 days. The most variable range is with P. malariae which can be from 18 to more than 40 days.

Note that P. vivax and P. ovale also may form hypnozoite forms which can remain in the liver for extended time periods and are responsible for relapsing illness that can be seen months after initial infection. (See primaquine in "Other treatment" below.)

Some merozoites differentiate into sexual forms, macro- and microgametocytes, and develop in erythrocytes. When an Anopheles mosquito feeds on an infected host and ingests the gametocytes, they migrate to the mosquito's stomach and combine to form zygotes and eventually oocysts. These oocysts enlarge and eventually rupture, releasing up to thousands of sporozoites into the mosquito's body. The sporozoites migrate to the salivary glands where they can then infect new hosts with subsequent blood meals. This Vector/Mosquito Phase may take 8 to 35 days depending on the species and environmental conditions.
Chemoprophylaxis and DEET-based mosquito repellants are effective in preventing malaria infection. A
Insecticide-treated bed nets are effective for reducing mortality. A

Though having a questionable benefit on mortality, a vaccine (RTS,S/AS01) showed modest efficacy against P. falciparum malaria infection in infants and children and the WHO has recommended large-scale pilot implementations of the vaccine in children 5-9 months of age in settings of moderate to high P. falciparum transmission in Africa. B
Medications for malaria chemoprophylaxis will vary based on the country and the specific epidemiology of that country. The CDC maintains and updates malaria prevention recommendations for travelers.

Authors of a Cochrane review found atovaquone-proguanil (250 mg/100 mg daily) and doxycycline (100 mg daily) to be the best tolerated regimen; mefloquine (250 mg weekly) is associated with adverse neuropsychiatric outcomes, though only has to be taken weekly.
Chloroquine (500mg weekly) or hydroxychloroquine (400mg weekly) can be considered in areas with known chloroquine-sensitive malaria.

Intermittent treatment to prevent malaria in preschool children living in endemic areas with seasonal malaria transmission prevents about three quarters of all clinical malaria episodes (rate ratio 0.26; 95% CI, 0.17-0.38).Intermittent treatment also likely produces a small reduction in all-cause mortality. No serious adverse drug events were reported in the 6 trials evaluated.

Two rounds of community-wide mass drug administration (MDA) and household-level (focal) MDA using dihydroartemisinin plus piperaquine compared with no mass treatment reduced malaria infection incidence and prevalence in low but not high-transmission areas in Zambia.

In areas where there are prevention and management services for malaria, Cochrane authors concluded that iron supplementation may reduce clinical malaria, although quality of evidence is poor.Based on higher quality evidence, iron and antimalarial treatment reduces clinical malaria (RR 0.54; 95% CI, 0.43-0.67; three trials, 728 children).

About 12% of pregnant women receiving chemoprophylaxis develop malaria infection during pregnancy compared with 24% of women receiving no drug (NNT 9; 95% CI, 5-31). In a database study conducted in 25 African countries, use of intermittent chemoprophylaxis or insecticide-treated mosquito nets for pregnant women was associated with a decreased risk of neonatal mortality and low birth weight.

In the setting of residential spraying of insecticides, adding monthly dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine to daily trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole did not reduce the risk of placental or maternal malaria or improve birth outcomes for HIV-infected pregnant African women.
In one RCT of 500 HIV-infected adults receiving ART, continuing vs. discontinuing cotrimoxazole resulted in lower malaria parasite prevalence of 4% compared to 22% at month 12.

A national Benin policy of providing intermittent sulfadoxine pyrimethamine treatment for pregnant women resulted in a rate of 10% low-birth-weight infants (8.7% was reported in the clinical trial conducted prior to national implementation) and a rate of malaria infection in the placenta of 11.2% (2.9% reported in the trial).

Intermittent treatment with 3 or more doses vs. a 2-dose regimen resulted in significantly lower rates of low-birth-weight infants with a NNT of 31 and an average 56 g higher mean birth weight. In this systematic review, there were no differences in serious adverse events between groups.
A new drug, DSM265, that selectively inhibits the parasite dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is under development.
Two monoclonal antibodies (L9LS and CIS43LS) that prevent infection have shown promising results in randomized trials.

The Environmental Protection Agency’s registered insect repellents including one of the following ingredients are recommended to prevent mosquito bites: Diethylmethyl-toluamide (DEET) (best protection), Picaridin (known as KBR 3023 and icaridin outside the US), IR3535, Oil of lemon eucalyptus, Para-menthane-diol (PMD), or 2-undecanon.

DEET-based mosquito repellants are effective in reducing bites and preventing infection when compared with placebo (OR 0.44; 95% CI, 0.25-0.76). They are safe for all age groups and should be at concentrations at least 25% or higher.
Picaradin and IR3535 (ethyl butylacetylamino-propionate) are also recommended by both the CDC and WHO.
Electronic mosquito repellants have no effect in preventing mosquito bites.

Use of metofluthrin mosquito coils may be effective in reducing malaria infections compared with placebo coils, but the benefit was no longer statistically significant when adjusting for intra-cluster correlation.
A randomized trial found that permethrin-treated baby wraps were successful at reducing the incidence of clinical malaria (0.73 versus 2.14 cases/100 person-weeks, p < 0.001).

Insecticide-treated bed nets reduce all-cause mortality in children in malaria-endemic areas; a saving of 5.6 lives (95% CI, 3.6 to 7.6) per year for every 1000 children protected with ITNs compared to no nets and possibly a benefit of 3.5 lives (95% CI, -2.4 to 6.8) each year for every 1000 children compared to use of non-treated nets.

In a 3-arm RCT comparing one of three types of long-lasting insecticidal net, greater protection from malaria was found using chlorfenapyr-pyrethroid nets compared to either pyrethroid-only or pyriproxyfen-pyrethroid nets (mean malarial incidence over 2 years of 0.56 cases per child-year, 1.03 cases per child-year and 0.84 cases per child-year, respectively).

A large prospective cohort study in Tanzania with 6706 children followed for 22 years found that use of mosquito nets before the age of 5 years significantly decreased the likelihood of death (adjusted hazard ratio 0.57, 95% CI 0.45 - 0.72).
Malaria vaccines are being investigated but are not currently available.

An RCT using RTS,S/AS01 in children found rates of first or only malaria episode at 12 months of 28% in children in the malaria vaccine group versus 41% for those in the rabies vaccine group. Common malaria vaccine complications included pneumonia, febrile convulsion, gastroenteritis, and falciparum malaria. In another RCT of African children aged 5 months to 17 months, the vaccine reduced the number of episodes of malaria from 1.08 per person-year to 0.55 per person-year (vaccine efficacy = 50.4%; 95% CI, 45.8%-54.6%).
Follow-up analysis of the 3-dose malaria vaccine (RTS,S/AS01) given at 5 to 17 months of age to African children did not result in reduced episodes of malaria by 7 years post administration.

However, in a 3-year 3-arm RCT enrolling 6861 children ages 5-17 months conducted in Mali and Bukina Faso, the incidence of clinical malaria per 1000 person-years at risk was 313 in the seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) alone group, 320 in the vaccine (RTS,S/AS01E)-alone group, and 133 in the combined SMC/vaccine group over 5 years. In addition, compared with the SMC group, combined SMC/vaccine reduced hospital admissions for severe malaria by 66.8% and for all-cause deaths by 44.5%.

A 3-dose vaccine (R21/Matrix-M) was tested against a control vaccine (rabies) in Africa in 5477 children and was found to be 68% to 75% effective and well tolerated at 12 months. In a second trial conducted in Bulina Faso, 3-dose R21/Matrix-M plus a booster was 71% effective in the low-dose adjuvant group and 80% effective in the high-dose adjuvant group against clinical malaria at one-year followup.

Use of solar-powered odor-baited mosquito trapping systems (SMoTS) may be helpful in preventing clinical malaria episodes. In a cluster-randomized trial, installing household SMoTS resulted in a reduced malaria prevalence of 23·7% (1552 of 6550 people) vs. 34.5% in non-intervened clusters (2002 of 5795 people) as measured by RDTs.

In one RCT, daily administration of 25 mg of zinc to pregnant women in Tanzania reduced risk of histopathology-positive placental malaria vs. with those who did not receive zinc, but did not reduce polymerase chain reaction-positive malaria, or delivery of premature or small-for-gestational-age infants.

Seasonal administration of Ivermectin en masse to individuals in communities where malaria incidence is high may reduce malaria incidence in children ages 5 years and under, without significant adverse reactions.

In theory, mass drug administration (MDA) should result in rapid reduction and eventual elimination of malaria in target populations, but MDA administration in low-transmission settings of sub-Saharan Africa has not consistently shown the ability to interrupt malaria transmission likely due to the high risk of re-introduction of malaria from imported malaria.
Suspect malaria in a patient with fever, chills, and myalgia with recent travel (within several months) to an endemic area. B
Light microscopy of Giemsa-stained blood smears is the gold standard for diagnosis. C
Other methods of rapid diagnostic testing are impractical for most countries with a high prevalence of malaria because of their cost. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Fever, headache, myalgias, lymphadenopathy, and short incubation (4-7 days)
Remittent fever, headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, and incubation from 3 to 60 days
Fever, headache, myalgias, and history of tick bite
Abdominal pain, jaundice, fever, and history of exposure
High fever, headache, myalgia, and vomiting

list.listitem: Suspect malaria in a patient with fever, chills, and myalgias with recent travel (within several months) to an endemic area. Almost all patients (98%) have fever. Over one-third of febrile patients with recent travel to the tropics have malaria.

In malaria-endemic areas, some patients develop partial immunity and may not become ill by the parasites; because of this, finding parasites in an ill patient does not mean that the illness is caused by the parasite.

In a systematic review, no specific symptoms or signs had sufficient accuracy to diagnose malaria. Of symptoms in travelers returning from endemic areas, fever (LR+ 5.1; 95% CI, 4.9-5.3) and lack of fever (LR− 0.12; 95% CI, 0.10-0.15) were most useful; on examination, splenomegaly (LR+ 6.5; 95% CI, 3.9-11), jaundice or icterus (LR+ 4.5; 95% CI, 1.7-12) moderately increased the likelihood of malaria.
Severe malaria is suspected in patients with confusion, coma, neurologic focal signs, severe anemia, respiratory difficulties.

Authors of a systematic review found a prevalence of respiratory distress syndrome of 2.8% in children and 2.2% in adults with Plasmodium vivax malaria; mortality was approximately 50% in these patients.

For those living in non-endemic areas, history of travel to malaria endemic areas is a key factor: 98% of patients with P. falciparum malaria will have symptoms within 3 months of travel, and 96% of patients with nonfalciparum malaria will have symptom onset within 12 months of travel.

Splenomegaly, the most common physical examination finding occurs in 22% of patients. Other manifestations of severe malaria include prostration, delirium, coma, respiratory distress, seizures, circulatory collapse, pulmonary edema, abnormal bleeding, and jaundice.

Black water fever is a clinical entity characterized by acute intravascular hemolysis classically occurring after intermittent use of quinine in long-term residents in Plasmodium falciparum endemic areas. Clinically, patients have fever, wine-colored urine, icterus, pallor, nausea, and acute renal failure from tubular necrosis.
With respect to laboratory tests, thrombocytopenia (LR+ 74; 9.2-601) and hyperbilirubinemia (LR+ 11; 8-15) increase the likelihood of malaria in travelers returning from endemic areas.

Recent testing using nucleic acids as biomarkers (Plasmodium 18S rRNA/rDNA nucleic acid tests) is promising showing earlier detection (7.6 days; 95% CI: 7.1-8.1 days) than blood smears (11.0 days; CI: 10.3-11.8 days) for malaria.
In another study, use of C-reactive protein (>2.4 mg/dL) and total bilirubin (>0.9 mg/dL) were useful in predicting malaria as opposed to dengue fever.
In many parts of the world, light microscopy of Giemsa-stained thick and thin blood films remains the best and most cost-effective test for detection and diagnosis of malaria parasitemia.

Light microscopy can detect as few as 5 to 10 malaria-infected erythrocytes per microliter of blood. Advantages include the low cost and the ability to determine parasite density, which can aid in prognosis. Disadvantages include its dependence upon individual expertise.,,

The malaria diagnostic competency assessment (MDCA) is a new initiative proposed by the MalariaCare project that recommends implementation of regular competency training for all personnel involved in histologic testing for malaria against country-specific minimum standards to ensure better detection using peripheral blood smears.
Rapid detection tests (RDTs)

The CDC notes that RDT is approved for use by hospital and commercial laboratories, not by individual clinicians or by patients themselves. They recommend that all RDTs be followed-up with microscopy to confirm results.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 74 trials, however, concluded that the sensitivity and specificity of all RDTs is such that they can replace or extend the access of diagnostic services for uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria.

Use of an RDT has been shown to reduce the proportion of patients with P. falciparum receiving inappropriate treatment compared with treatment based on clinical diagnosis. In addition, vivax-specific RDTs appear to be highly sensitive and specific when compared with microscopy for detecting P vivax malaria.
In another study, compared to histopathology, use of a latent class analysis approach improved RDT sensitivity from 79.5% in peripheral and 66.2% in placental blood to 93.7% and 80.2%, respectively.
Because the Histidine-rich protein 2 (HRP-2) antigen persists even after effective treatment, it is not useful for detecting treatment failures.

An HRP2 test (Binax NOW Malaria test) performed well (sensitivity for P. falciparum 97.7%, specificity 99.6%) in a sample of travellers presenting to the emergency department in Sweden but for nonfalciparum species, sensitivity was only 58.3%.
A novel ultrasensitive RDT for P. falciparum was not superior to conventional RDT testing.

Another novel malaria antigen detection system, the XN-30 hematology analyzer, has shown superior sensitivity and specificity when compared to microscopy (98.7% and 99. 4%). The accuracy for the XN-30 for microscopic malaria was equal to or higher than HRP-2 and plasmomodium lactate dehydrogenase (pLDH) RDTs, respectively.
The HRP2 test is currently the only FDA-approved rapid malaria diagnostic test for P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. malariae, or P. ovale.
HRP2 antigen testing may be falsely negative using conventional RDT's in patients with low parasitic density levels.

Parasite nucleic acids can be detected using polymerase chain reaction. This technique may be slightly more sensitive than smear microscopy but is not readily available, especially in limited resource countries.

In two studies, a portable device using the loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) method for malaria diagnosis with simple DNA extraction had high sensitivity and specificity compared to RDTs and the standard LAMP-Thermocyler.
Serology can detect antibodies indicating past exposure to malaria parasites, using either indirect immunofluorescence or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay
In laboratories that are unfamiliar with malaria diagnosis, the CDC maintains an inquiries service (https://www.cdc.gov/dpdx/index.html or print the form and FAX to +1 404-718-4195).
See for a suggested approach to diagnosing malaria.
Treatment is based on the infecting organism, clinical status (uncomplicated vs. severe), and parasite drug susceptibility (CDC 2013).

Severe infection is determined by one or more of the following: impaired consciousness/coma, severe normocytic anemia (hemoglobin <7 g/dL), renal failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome, hypotension, disseminated intravascular coagulation, spontaneous bleeding, acidosis, hemoglobinuria, jaundice, repeated generalized convulsions, and/or parasitemia of ≥5%.
Area of acquisition of infection helps narrow the Plasmodium parasite species implicated and aids in determining the likelihood of drug resistance.
A medicine used in failed chemoprophylaxis should not be a part of the treatment regimen.

Antimalarial treatment effective against chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum should be initiated if the diagnosis is suspected but can’t be confirmed or the diagnosis is confirmed but species determination is not possible.
The World Health Organization (WHO) and CDC maintain up-to-date guidelines for the treatment of malaria, including resistant and multiple-drug resistant strains.
Artemisinin-based treatment combination therapies are considered standard of care by WHO guidelines for treatment in P. falciparum malaria endemic areas, with cure rates exceeding 95%. A
For non-falciparum malaria, chloroquine is an option if chloroquine resistance is not a concern in the patient's region. A
For severe malaria, IV or IM artesunate for 24 hours followed by 3 days of oral combination therapy is recommended by WHO guidelines. B
The WHO and CDC maintain up-to-date guidelines for the treatment of malaria, including resistant and multiple-drug-resistant strains.
It is important to determine the species of Plasmodium (falciparum or non-falciparum) and the country in which malaria was acquired. Both will help guide the type of medication used.

Artemisinin-based treatment combination therapies are considered standard of care by WHO guidelines for treatment in P. falciparum malaria endemic areas, with cure rates exceeding 95%. Combinations recommended by WHO (2022) include artemether + lumefantrine, artesunate + amodiaquine, artesunate + mefloquine, dihydroartemisinin + piperaquine, and artesunate + sulfadoxine–pyrimethamine. Patients should receive 3 days of the artemisinin derivative.

For patients with non-falciparum malaria (P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae or P. knowlesi), artemisinin-based combination therapy is also recommended by WHO guidelines. Chloroquine is an option for patients in chloroquine sensitive regions.
For severe malaria, IV or IM artesunate for 24 hours followed by 3 days of oral combination therapy is recommended by WHO guidelines.

In the Americas, primaquine is recommended to prevent relapse of P lasmodium vivax malaria following treatment with chloroquine. A randomized trial in Brazil found that 7.0 mg/kg of primaquine was more effective than 3.5 mg/kg at preventing relapse (86% versus 59% without recurrence, p < 0.001, NNT = 4).
There are reports in Southeast Asia of artemisinin resistance in Plasmodium falciparum; increasing duration of treatment to 6 days resulted in high cure rates in one report.
Authors of a Cochrane review of 2 small trials of intramuscular artesunate versus quinine for severe malaria found similar outcomes but little power to detect important differences.

Artesunate plus mefloquine is more effective than mefloquine alone for treating uncomplicated falciparum malaria in areas with low malaria transmission.Doses of 25 mg/kg mefloquine and at least 10 mg artesunate resulted in higher cure rates.

In an RCT with 252 Malaysian patients infected with Plasmodium knowlesi malaria, artesunate-mefloquine was more effective than chloroquine for parasite clearance (84% vs. 55%), with faster fever clearance and a lower rate of anemia at 28 days (62% vs. 75%). There was one case of a serious neuropsychiatric event with artesunate-mefloquine.
Azithromycin is a weak antimalarial and not as effective as current antimalarial treatment.
An RCT in 1271 patients with P. falciparum malaria found that pyronaridine-artesunate was non-inferior to mefloquine plus artesunate.

Interventions shown to increase adherence to antimalarial drugs include packaging aids, visual media, combined visual media and verbal information, community education, medication supervision, and convenient regimens.
Primaquine is the recommended drug to prevent P. vivax relapses and 7 days of therapy (1 mg/kg/day) is non-inferior to 14 days of therapy (0.5 mg/kg/day).
In one study a G6PD rapid diagnostic test was reasonably accurate for screening to identify individuals with enzyme activities below 60%.
An osmotic diuretic (mannitol 20%) was not effective in reducing death or neurologic sequelae in a single trial of children with cerebral malaria.
In the United States, patients with suspected malaria should be hospitalized and treated empirically until diagnostic testing is done.

Patients with severe malaria require parenteral treat and have the following symptoms: impaired consciousness/coma, severe normocytic anemia (hemoglobin <7 g/dL), renal failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome, hypotension, disseminated intravascular coagulation, spontaneous bleeding, acidosis, hemoglobinuria, jaundice, repeated generalized convulsions, and/or parasitemia of ≥5%.

Parenteral treatment with quinidine gluconate (6.25 mg base/kg loading dose over 1-2 hours, then 0.0125 mg base/kg/min continuous infusion) should be initiated for patients with severe malaria if parenteral artesunate is not available.
P. ovale and P. vivax have a dormant liver stage, hypnozoites, which may cause relapses for up to many months after initial infection. B
Of the 5 strains that infect humans, P. falciparum has the capability to rapidly progress to severe illness or death. B
Fever will generally break within about 72 hours (if responding to treatment). C
Repeat blood smears should be done to monitor effectiveness of treatment. C

Among patients with complicated malaria (cerebral malaria, hypoglycemia, anemia, jaundice, and renal failure), about half will develop multiple complications, the first typically developing within 5 days of onset of fever. B

In a study of 454 patients in Pakistan, neurologic involvement was seen in 27 of 123 patients (22%) with complicated malaria and 43 of 331 patients (13%) with uncomplicated malaria. Of the 16 (4%) patients who died, 13 had complicated malaria and 3 had uncomplicated malaria; mortality was significantly higher among patients with versus without neurological involvement (13% vs. 2%, respectively).
Complications typically progress from one complication to another every 72 hours, with mortality increasing from 15% in those with a single complication to 100% in those with 5 or more. B

In a study of 83 Malawian children with retinopathy-positive cerebral malaria versus 95 controls, children with cerebral malaria had total developmental delay on the Malawi Developmental Assessment Tool, with the greatest effects on language development; coma duration, seizures in hospital, platelet count, and lactate level on admission were predictive of assessment outcomes.
Malaria infection during pregnancy is associated with increased risk for spontaneous abortion, premature delivery, congenital infection, and neonatal death.

Children born to mothers with placental malaria, but not children born to mothers with peripheral infection without evidence of placental sequestration, have an increased risk of malaria during the first year of life compared with children born to mothers with no malaria during pregnancy.

For women in their first or second pregnancy, malaria chemoprevention reduces the risk of moderate to severe anemia by about 40% (RR 0.60; 95% CI, 0.47-0.75) and antenatal parasitemia by about 61% (RR 0.39; 95% CI, 0.26-0.58).Infants of women who receive chemoprevention have increased birth weight (mean 93 g).

In an open-label, three-arm, cluster-randomized, superiority trial conducted in Indonesia including 2279 pregnant women, those randomized to either a strategy of intermittent preventive treatment (IPT) with dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine or intermittent screening and the same treatment (IST) had lower rates of malaria prevalence at delivery than single screening and treatment (SST) of 11.6%, 10.6%, and 20.2%, respectively. However, malaria prevalence was lower at enrollment in the IST group (5·7%) compared to SST (12·6%) and IPT (10·6%) clusters.

In high resistance areas, the incidence of symptomatic malaria during pregnancy was significantly lower with intermittent preventive treatment using 3-dose dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine or monthly dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine compared to sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine. Adverse birth outcomes were also lower in the dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine group compared to the other two groups (9.2% vs. 18.6% in the sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine group and 21.3% in the dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine group).

Monthly intermittent preventive treatment with dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine as an alternative to sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine during pregnancy, though safe, does not lead to significant improvements in outcomes compared to sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine.
There are scant high-quality data on the safety and effectiveness of treating malaria during pregnancy.
Treating pregnant women infected with P. falciparum malaria with quinine plus clindamycin is as effective as artesunate.

Quinine, chloroquine, clindamycin, proguanil, and mefloquine are all considered safe during the first trimester of pregnancy. Though artemesinin combination therapies are not recommended as first line treatments in the first trimester unless cases are severe or other therapies are unavailable, they are recommended during the remainder of pregnancy.

However, authors of a systematic review comparing artemisinin-based combination therapies with non-artemisinin therapies administered in the first trimester found no differences in adverse pregnancy outcomes (adjusted hazard ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.49-1.03) including embryotoxicity or teratogenicity based on the risk of miscarriage, stillbirth, or major congenital anomalies. Treatment in the first trimester may reduce risk of low birthweight.

In one RCT of 4 different artesunate regimens with 3428 pregnant women who had falciparum malaria, all treatments resulted in high cure rates (94.2%-98%) with amodiaquine-artesunate, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine, and mefloquine-artesunate showing slightly higher cure rates than artemether-lumefantrine. The latter drug provided the fewest adverse effects but the shortest post-treatment prophylaxis.
For those with chloroquine-sensitive strains, chloroquine treatment should be used as it is for non-pregnant patients.

Primaquine use during pregnancy for treatment of hypnozoites (P. vivax and P. ovale) should be avoided and weekly chloroquine prophylaxis should be initiated if P. vivax or P. ovale infection is confirmed. As primaquine can pass into breast milk, nursing women should avoid primaquine unless infants have known normal G6PD levels.

In a retrospective case series of 213 cases of severe falciparum malaria in pregnancy managed between 1980 and 2020 in Southeast Asia, the mean maternal age was 25.7, mean gestational age was 25.6 weeks, overall maternal mortality was 12.2% and fetal loss was 23.3%. Three factors were associated with increased maternal mortality – coma, hypotension and respiratory failure.

In a case series of 523 children in Uganda treated for severe malaria, 7.5% died. Intestinal fatty-acid binding protein, a marker of intestinal injury was elevated in 415 (795) and higher levels were associated with lower systolic blood pressure, increasing stage of acute kidney injury, coma, and a 7.4-fold higher relative risk of in-hospital death.

Among 757 infants born to women enrolled in the Indonesian trial comparing IPT, IST and SST, there was no difference in incidence rates of clinical malaria for those randomized to intermittent preventive treatment with curative dose of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine compared to passive case detection (24% and 19%, respectively) or parasitemia at 12 months (13% and 16%, respectively).
In areas highly endemic for malaria, school-based screening of Malawian primary schools identified a prevalence of infection by RDT screening of 37% (9%-64% among schools).
Tetracycline and doxycycline have a relative contraindication for children younger than 8 years. Therefore, quinine plus clindamycin should be used instead.

The CDC recommends atovaquone-proguanil; artemether-lumefantrine; oral quinine sulfate plus doxycycline, tetracycline, or clindamycin; or oral mefloquine as treatment options for children with P. falciparum in chloroquine-resistant or unknown resistance areas.

In a RTC among 747 Nigerian children <5 years of age with uncomplicated malaria, 3-day regimens of artemether-lumefantrine or artesunate-amodiaquine performed similarly for safety and tolerability, with an overall efficacy of 96.3% (95% CI, 94.5%-97.6%).
Clinicians should be aware of the possibility of delayed hemolysis in children treated with parenteral artesunate for severe malaria; in one cohort study, this occurred in 7% of 72 children.

Artemether-lumefantrine (AL) and dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine showed excellent treatment efficacy for uncomplicated malaria in Ugandan children (6 months - 5 years) in spite of recent increases in P. falciparum resistance to artemisinins and piperaquine.
Chloroquine (dose adjusted for weight) can safely be used in children for any chloroquine-sensitive malaria strains.

Malaria likely. Microscopist experienced in malaria diagnosis?
Do peripheral blood stained with Giemsa.
Do rapid assay and confirm if positive. (Send blood smear to experienced laboratory or contact CDC at dpdx@cdc.gov or 770-448-7788.)
